M O R E   M A I L ! !


   August, 1992      Page Reply

 How to write to us...02     -
 Edward G. Collier....03    05
 R. Webster...........07    08
 Malcolm Perry........09    17
 W.A. Yates...........18    21
 Malcolm Goodman......22    24
 L.G. Baumann.........25    27
 Carlo Maria Vireca...32     -
 M.D. Atkins..........44    49

   PLEASE SEND YOUR TEXTFILE!
Text is accepted in any form for
OUTLETTERS: wordprocessor files
(say which),typed or handwritten
letters. However, PLEASE send us
a textfile if possible so your
letter needn't be typed again!
The easiest for us to edit are
Tasword 2 files with the right
margin set at 32 but a textfile
in ANY format is appreciated!

Please state if there should be
parts of your letter you do not
wish published but we always use
our discretion anyway. Letters
may also be edited for clarity
and length... Please ask if you
welcome direct correspondence
from other OUTLET readers and we
will publish your full address.

From: E.G. Collier, HEREFORD

Dear Ron and Brian,


        BIBLE PROGRAM

Thank you for taking such
trouble with my Bible program
and for the excellent
introduction. Unfortunately, on
the +3 version at least, your
alterations have, I suspect,
over-filled the memory. As a
result, if one tries to break
into the program to LIST or
SAVE it, the program crashes
and produces some fine Chinese
characters on the screen. I at
least am unable to get past
this barrier.

I wonder whether you might be
able to re-issue the program
later and perhaps delete one
keyword and its text so that
there is a little latitude in
memory to enable people to SAVE
the program and adapt it for
their own uses. I will send you
my MISCINF program soon that
uses the same dodge but has an
alphabetic system to enable one
to file data alphabetically
very easily and to make a
back-up automatically before
adding, deleting or amending
any data, if desired.

       Yours sincerely,

      Edward G. Collier

Brian Cavers to Edward G.Collier

Firstly, all credit for "taking
such trouble" with editing many
of our readers' programs must go
to Chris Oliver who has helped
us ENORMOUSLY in this respect.

As for "BIBLE", the "chinese
characters" problem is not due
to the memory being over-filled
(at least, not directly) but to
a design fault (or probably more
fair to say a design LIMITATION)
of 128K BASIC. In 128K BASIC,any
new character set positioned in
memory above address 49152 gets
paged out when you enter the 128
editor so the character shapes
are taken from the wrong part of
memory - resulting in jumbled up
hieroglyphics!

The answer is to reset your +3
or any 128K Spectrum, enter 128K
(+3) BASIC and enter...

        MERGE "BIBLE.DAT"

You may have to wait a minute or
so while a big program like
BIBLE loads but when it has you
will find it does not auto-run
but just says "O.K." and then
you can list it clearly. You can
then study it, alter it etc. but
if you run it and then use BREAK
the listing will be jumbled
again because our character set
is built-in. To permanently
remove it enter:  9994 RETURN
and then: RUN 9972 to resave the
program (but lose our nice,thick
characters for the normal ones!)
                         - Brian

From: M. Perry, KIDDERMINSTER

Dear Brian and Ron,

In answer to the question from
Mark Longthorn on the +D drive
connector, the pin layout is as
follows - also true for Disciple
and SAM external drive adaptor
(except, I believe, D1/2 select
is different in that the drive
is left as D1 and the select is
done in the interface).

Looking at the rear of the +D
the pins are numbered from right
to left with all odd numbers on
top and even numbers on bottom.

33 31 ........ 5 3 1
34 32 ........ 6 4 2

All the top row, odd numbers are
EARTHS ( 0V )

On the bottom row, all even
numbers are as follows. Note NU
= not used. "+" represents +D is
outputting data or a signal to
control drive and "-" means it
is a drive status signal or data
into +D.
    2   NU
    4   NU
    6   NU
    8 - INDEX
   10 + DRIVE ONE SELECT
   12 + DRIVE TWO SELECT
   14   NU
   16 + MOTOR ON
   18 + STEP DIRECTION
   20 + STEP SIGNAL
   22 + DATA OUT, WRITE

   24 + WRITE GATE
   26 - TRACK ZERO
   28   NU
   30 - DATA IN, READ
   32 + SELECT SIDE
   34   NU

The plug on the rear of the
drive is the same format as
above except that pins marked NU
carry signals that the +D does
not use e.g. pin 14 can be drive
3 select. Obviously, direction
of signals "+" represents into
drive and "-" signal out of
drive.

The pins are at 5V level for
"off" or not selected and pulled
down to 0V for function active
or select.

The 26 pin printer plug is also
numbered as above and
connections are:-
1, strobe. All odd 3 to 17 inc.
data bits 0 to 7 res. 21 busy
All even 2 to 22 inc.earth (0V).
Odds 19 to 25 inc and 24 & 26
are not used.

DIRECTORIES. The mention of CAT
1 "x" is the selective directory
listing form.Not well documented
as I recall in the handbooks.


A specific name such as "TEST"
would only list the program
"TEST" if there is one. "TEST*"
would list all files starting
with TEST such as TEST1,TEST2
TESTING and so on.

The "?" can also be used as for
example "??R*" would only list
files that have"R" as the third
letter. Just to recap on "*" and
"?" The "?" means "this can be
any character", the "*" means
"this character can be anything
and any following are ignored".
That is why ERASE "*" wipes the
entire disc and the characters
"*" and "?" can cause problems
if used in file names.
E.g. say a file name of "*this"
was put on disc. now try and
erase with "*this": disaster - a
blank disc! Remember the rule
"*" this can be anything and
ignore everything after so erase
all files with any first char-
acter and ignore any trailing
characters.

"?this" would only erase "*this"
and any other 5 letter name with
"THIS" as the last 4 characters.
Incidentally,on a blank disc,try
SAVE d1 "*ONE". Now try and save
"*TWO" It asks if you want to
overwrite "*ONE"! There must be
a use for this somewhere but
indicates why the * and ? should
not be used in file names.

I have recently found that the
5V supply to my SAM is somewhat
unstable and falls towards 4.5V
on disc operation, also varied
due to poor connection of the
power input 6 pin plug. The
obvious visible signs are flick-
ering and changes of brightness
of screen, there could well be
less obvious effects.

The disc control IC to name one
is stated as 5V +/- 5% which
gives it a lower limit of 4.75V
the 5V rail is going below this
specification. Is this a reason
for some of the drive problems I
wonder?

What other ICs or even drives
are being expected to run with a
5V rail that goes below their
specification limits I ask. I
know from experience certain
drives failed to work reliably
if the supply fell below about
4.7V.

I believe the volt drop could be
due to the somewhat thin
multicore cable between PSU and
computer.

This fall in voltage on load
would be even worse if things
such as audio amps, card cage
without extra PSU and etc.  are
also drawing on the 5V rail of
SAM. As my machine is still both
under guarantee and the subject
of a dispute, I refrained from
checking to see how stable the
5V is in the PSU itself to prove
the cable theory. It would be
interesting though to check the
5V supply on a machine that is
playing up and running it from a
more stable supply. Note I am
not recommending you go poking
voltages into SAM 'cos as a
certain person in a TV show says
"they don't like it up 'em they
don't " unless you know what you
are doing.       - Malcolm Perry

Brian Cavers to Malcolm Perry

I don't think I realized that
ERASE "*THIS" would erase every-
thing on the disc! I don't use
"*" in filenames although I
don't think I make a conscious
effort not to do so - rather
it's just not a symbol I would
gener- ally use in a filename.
Let's hope I remember!

One other symbol that has caused
me minor inconvenience is the
"/" character.This has been used
by readers in filenames of text
files and Masterdos doesn't like
it of course. I forget the error
message but it does prevent one
loading them without SAMDOS!
                       - Brian

From: Malcolm Goodman, LEEDS

Your editorial in last month's
OUTLET made depressing reading.
I hope it was a one-off blip in
sales as I believe that there
are many who need a monthly
"fix" of OUTLET.

Now, onto your reply about how
to "interrogate" what has been
assigned to numeric or string
variables.Your suggestion's fine
for numerics, but if you let V$=
"hello" then use V$ in the INPUT
prompt, then the answer you get
is "V$" and not "hello". Try it,
and you will realise why I set
the problem in the first place.
I believe it still remains a
good programming puzzle.

Lastly, your comments about code
location in the SAM. One
possible answer is the 'LOCATOR'
routine published by John Pitts
in Issue One of 'SOFTRIX'. It is
not PD so if it's what you want
then you'll need to contact him.

           Regards,

            Malcolm

Brian Cavers to Malcolm Goodman


Ah! - I see now what you mean!
If the INPUT string variable is
the same as the one you want to
investigate then it will destroy
it! Mr. L.G. Baumann spotted my
mistake too so I will reply more
fully on this whole puzzle after
the next letter.

Thanks for the LOCATOR info. It
is not quite what I had in mind
but was of interest anyway. Pity
this routine isn't PD as it does
severely limit its usefulness!

                        - Brian

From: L. G. Baumann, STH. AFRICA

Dear Brian,

Malcolm Goodman raised a problem
on variables in your OUTLETTERS
of July 1992 to which you gave a
possible solution.Unfortunately,
your suggested program destroys
the value already held in the
string V$.

I think it is necessary to park
the value of V$ in a temporary
home and restore it to its value
later.

Perhaps the following changes to
your listing will be of some
help (assuming the variables
have already all been declared):

 10 LET temp = VAL V$: INPUT
    "Variable? ";V$
 20 IF V$ = "V$" THEN LET V$ =
    STR$ temp
 30 IF V$ (LEN V$ = "$" THEN
    PRINT VAL$ V$: LET V$ =
    STR$ temp: GO TO 10
 40 PRINT VAL V$: LET V$ =  STR$
    temp: GO TO 10

I will be interested to see the
other solutions that will be
given.

          L.G.Baumann

Brian Cavers to L.G. Baumann

Yes,I see my mistake but you are
making the assumption that the
string variables contain only
numerals whereas they may have
text which would crash with your
solution with "variable not
found". The idea of storing the
variable first seems promising
though. Perhaps one could POKE
it into memory, character by
character and then read it back.
However, this would be slow with
a very large string and care
would have to be taken not to
POKE memory used by something
else - not ideal for a universal
solution as this wants to be.
This is a good puzzle and I have
one more possible solution...

First, for other readers who may
not have seen Malcolm Goodman's
letter last month, the puzzle is
to write a BASIC routine that
would let you enter the name of
any of (previously-declared) 26
numeric variables and 26 strings
for each letter of the alphabet
and have it printed up, e.g.,you
would enter X and it would print
99 (if x=99) or enter Z$ and it
would print "hello" (if z$ is
"hello").

After Malcolm's and your letters
this month I went back to the
wording of Malcolm's first
challenge and noticed he didn't
state INPUT as such. I began to
wonder what other ways are there
of entering anything into the
computer from the keyboard...

I can only think of INKEY$ but
it would still seem to need a
string variable to store its
value. Of course, SAM has GET as
well but the same applies.

Incidentally on SAM, my previous
solution would work if the INPUT
used a 2-letter string variable
name like VV$ or a long weird
name like QZOGKUQQ$ would let it
work with any reasonable name.
However, for this puzzle I am
sticking to a universal solution
that will work on either SAM or
Spectrum.

I've been racking my brains and
I think I have a way to store
INKEY$ without a variable but I
have not tried it so here goes..

10 DECLARE VARIABLES ETC...
20 CLS : PRINT "VARIABLE? "
20 PAUSE 0:PRINT INKEY$;
30 PAUSE 0:PRINT INKEY$
40 IF SCREEN$(1,1)=" " THEN
   PRINT VAL SCREEN$(1,0): STOP
60 IF SCREEN$(1,0)="A" THEN
   PRINT A$
70 IF SCREEN$(1,0)="B" THEN
   PRINT B$
   ETC. ETC...

As I was typing this I could see
my original plan would not work
out. I had hoped to use say...
PRINT VAL$(SCREEN$(1,0)+ SCREEN$
(1,1)) but the SCREEN$ bug stops
any string slicing without first
storing in a variable so needing
at least TWO string variables to
get more than one character off
the screen.

I must admit I'm stuck for the
moment. I suppose one could POKE
the BASIC line directly to alter
a PRINT statement.

I'll give it some more thought.
Anyone else care to try!!??

                        - Brian

       Carlo Maria VIRECA
  Via G. Di Vittorio 38 20026
     Novate Milanese ITALY

This letter may contain, I hope,
some information useful for
Dominic Morris in relation to
his letter in OUTLET 58. I don't
own a +3 so have not understood
Morris's problem but I have
hacked OCP assembler to get a
listing on a normal printer.

I'm not sure what he means with
'unfortunately the program still
clears the printer buffer...'.
My OCP Assembler version uses
the printer buffer in many ways:
-as printer buffer like it is;
-for temporary storing (e.g.
when verifying, loading, and so
on...).

In my OCP's Assembler there are
at least 2 subroutine to clear
the printer buffer: first at
27960-72, second at 29571-29583.

I own an OCP FULL SCREEN EDITOR/
ASSEMBLER, OXFORD COMPUTER PUB-
LISHING LIMITED 1983, written by
JAMES HUTCHBY, with 36 pages
manual, for SPECTRUM 16k & 48k
and my system is: SPECTRUM 48K
rubber keyboard + DISCIPLE +
drive + Amstrad 24-pin printer.

1) OCP controls the presence of
ZX-dedicated-printer at
27928-27932 and at 33098-33103.
To disable these two tests I
have used 3 POKEs:
POKE 27932,0 - was 192 ret nz
POKE 33102,0 - was 32
POKE 33103,0 - was 27 jr nz

2) OCP clears and fills the
printer buffer in different
ways, too hard to modify, but
when the buffer is filled with
the contents to be passed to the
printer it makes 2 calls to the
'COPY-BUFF' ROM SUBROUTINE:
first at 28005, second at 33149
both JP 3789 or JP 0ECDh: I have
redirected the JUMPs to my own
copy-buffer subroutine.

3) I have assembled my own copy-
buffer subroutine at 23760 then
I have inserted the code in a
line   1 REM .... added to the
OCP basic;there is not much room
but line 50 and line 100 may be
deleted.  My routine for 24-pin
is 112 bytes long but a routine
for 8-pin printer should be
shorter.

4) To redirect the JPs I have
simply POKEd at 28006-7 and at
33150-1 the starting address of
my routine: 23760.

5) I have saved all BASIC and
modified code with a snapshot.
On the same disc I have saved an
AUTOLOAD BASIC program that,
before reloading the snapshotted
OCP, sets my system to right
paper feed rate and to send
unchanged codes to the printer
(POKE @6,1 with Disciple).

Pnumber option and/LP switch
both work properly with this
change. In my driver I have
fired only first 16 pins so I
get up to 120 rows of listing on
an A4 sheet of paper.

The printer buffer starting at
23296 contains 256 bytes: 8
lines * 32 bytes each.

This is the assembler listing of
my 24-pin driver to copy the
printer buffer:

      org  23760

start push ix     (for caution)
      ld   a,3    open printer
      call 1601h  channel
      ld   a,27
      rst  10h
      ld   a,42      set triple
      rst  10h
      ld   a,39      density
      rst  10h
      ld   a,0
      rst  10h

      ld   a,2    512=each pixel
      rst  10h    printed twice
      ld   b,32   loop x32 bytes
      ld   hl,23296    p.buffer
cex   push bc
      push hl
      ld   b,8    loop bit7 bit0
cor   push bc
      push hl
      xor  a
      ld   b,8    loop x8 pixel
      ld   de,32          lines
cve   rlc  (hl)
      rla           move to 'a'
      add  hl,de    a vertical
      djnz cve      byte
      ld   (ori),a
      ld   hl,ori
      ld   de,dup   then double
      ld   b,2      the vertical
two   push bc       byte
.

      ld   b,4
      xor  a
qua   rlc  (hl)
      rla
      rrc  (hl)
      rlc  (hl)
      rla          and store the
      djnz qua     the doubled
      ld   (de),a  byte in 'dup'
      inc  de      & in 'dup+1'
      pop  bc
      djnz two
      ld   b,2     print twice
sec   push bc      the doubled
      ld   a,(dup)  byte
      rst  10h
      ld   a,(dup+1)
      rst  10h
      xor  a       leaving empty
      rst  10h     last 8 pin
      pop  bc

      djnz sec
      pop  hl
      pop  bc      next pixel
      djnz cor
      pop  hl
      inc  hl      next byte
      pop  bc
      djnz cex
      ld   a,13
      rst  10h     carr.return
      ld   a,10
      rst  10h     line feed
      pop  ix
      ret          return


ori   defb 0
dup   defw 0

end

This routine needs to set paper
feed rate, from basic, to 15/180
inch to avoid streaking between
lines: e.g. LPRINT char 27,51,15
--------------------------------

This is the assembler listing of
an 8-pin driver I think should
work to copy the printer buffer:

      org  23760

start push ix     (for caution)
      ld   a,3    open printer
      call 1601h  channel
      ld   a,27
      rst  10h
+     ld   a,76   to set double
      rst  10h    density graph.
      ld   a,0
      rst  10h

++    ld   a,2   512=each pixel
      rst  10h   printed twice
      ld   b,32  loop x32 bytes
      ld   hl,23296  p.buffer
cex   push bc
      push hl
      ld   b,8   loop bit7 bit0
cor   push bc
      push hl
      xor  a
      ld   b,8    loop x8 pixel
      ld   de,32          rows
cve   rlc  (hl)
      rla           move to 'a'
      add  hl,de    a vertical
      djnz cve      byte
+++   push af
+++   rst  10h      print twice
+++   pop  af       the vertical
      rst  10h      byte
      pop  hl

      pop  bc      next pixel
      djnz cor
      pop  hl
      inc  hl      next char
      pop  bc
      djnz cex
      ld   a,13
      rst  10h     carr.return
      ld   a,10
      rst  10h     line feed
      pop  ix
      ret          return

end
+) If you like single density
the routine is easy to modify
(75 instead of 76)
++) Printing once the vertical
    byte: ld a,1 to send 256
    bytes only  and no need
    all +++) lines.

That's all.

Thanks for your precious work

              Carlo Maria VIRECA

From: M.D. Atkins, BURY

I have just read the editorial
concerning the future of OUTLET
and I'm sure I'll be one of many
who will be very disappointed if
you are forced to cease publish-
ing what I consider to be the
best-ever Spectrum magazine.
During the six months that I
have been a member, the content
of OUTLET has been such that I
have acquired all the back
issues of the +3 version.

I've noticed a number of adverts
which appear to indicate some of
the more active members who have
regularly contributed to OUTLET
are changing to systems other
than SAM.

This surprises me as I do not
consider the alternatives offer
value for money particularly
when taking into account the
price of the software.

At work, I have the opportunity
to use a 486, which runs AUTOCAD
and WORKS to name but two of the
programs, and due to the nature
of the work a very expensive
monitor is used. The quality of
the graphics is far superior to
any system that I could
reasonably afford to have at
home and for that reason alone I
am not inclined to change my +3.
Who needs the more sophisticated
and expensive programs for home
use when adequate software
exists for the Spectrum?

Resolving various Spectrum bugs
and modifying software such as
Tasword and Wordmaster all add
to the fun and most of these
modifications have only been
possible through Outlet.

I hope you do not have to make
any dramatic changes to OUTLET
within the foreseeable future
but, if necessary, I would be
prepared to accept a bi-monthly
edition or even a price increase
should you consider this to be
the only answer. Enough of the
doom and gloom now lets get to
the fun of owning a Spectrum.

I am still attempting to make
back-up copies of OUTLET on 3.5"
discs. [from PLUS 3, 3" discs]

In order to save time I am using
Brian Gaff's file maintenance
utility and placing each edition
in a different user area. This
has enabled me to get round the
problem caused by CAT listing
only the first 64 files.

In doing this I have noticed
some of the files "grow" by 1K
when transferred to drive B. I
have also noticed when there are
more than 25 files in the third
or fourth user area the capacity
of the 3.5" disc becomes
noticeably less than 706K i.e.
the disc space used plus the
disc space remaining is less
than 706K. This completely rules
out planning which programs can
be stored on the back-up.

I have followed Brian Gaff's
advice and just got hold of a
second-hand copy of Locomotive's
CP/M Plus and Mallard BASIC. I
don't know yet whether this will
do the back-ups without showing
this annoying error.

Do you know of any utilities
similar to D.I.C.E. which exist
for second drives?

          M.D. Atkins

Brian Cavers to M.D. Atkins

I've never used D.I.C.E so don't
know the details of its features
but I believe one of its main
capabilities is as a disc sector
editor. Our own EDIS (OUTLET 51)
is a good +3 sector editor but I
have never tried it on larger
format discs. I don't know of
any other software. Are you
saying that D.I.C.E. does not
work on Drive B?That seems a bit
restrictive - or is that it just
doesn't work with large formats?

Regarding the problem with CAT
listing only 64 files there is a
great utility called CATCHUP in
next month's OUTLET which should
give you a full CAT!
                     - Brian.

From: E.G. Collier, HEREFORD

In answer to the question from Mark Longthorn on the +D drive connector, the pin layout is as follows - also true for Disciple and SAM external drive adaptor (except, I believe, D1/2 select is different in that the drive is left as D1 and the select is done in the interface).

Looking at the rear of the +D the pins are numbered from right to left with all odd numbers on top and even numbers on bottom.

```text
33 31 ........ 5 3 1
34 32 ........ 6 4 2
```

All the top row, odd numbers are EARTHS ( 0V )

On the bottom row, all even numbers are as follows. Note NU = not used. "+" represents +D is outputting data or a signal to control drive and "-" means it is a drive status signal or data into +D.

```text
    2   NU
    4   NU
    6   NU
```

8 - INDEX 10 + DRIVE ONE SELECT 12 + DRIVE TWO SELECT

```text
   14   NU
```

16 + MOTOR ON 18 + STEP DIRECTION 20 + STEP SIGNAL 22 + DATA OUT, WRITE

24 + WRITE GATE 26 - TRACK ZERO

```text
   28   NU
```

30 - DATA IN, READ 32 + SELECT SIDE

```text
   34   NU
```

The plug on the rear of the drive is the same format as above except that pins marked NU carry signals that the +D does not use e.g. pin 14 can be drive 3 select. Obviously, direction of signals "+" represents into drive and "-" signal out of drive.

The pins are at 5V level for "off" or not selected and pulled down to 0V for function active or select.

The 26 pin printer plug is also numbered as above and connections are:- 1, strobe. All odd 3 to 17 inc. data bits 0 to 7 res. 21 busy All even 2 to 22 inc.earth (0V). Odds 19 to 25 inc and 24 & 26 are not used.

В ответ на вопрос Mark Longthorn о разъеме дисковода +D привожу цоколевку контактов — она также актуальна для Disciple и адаптера внешнего привода SAM (за исключением того, что, как мне кажется, выбор D1/2 там отличается тем, что привод всегда остается D1, а выбор осуществляется в самом интерфейсе).

Если смотреть на заднюю панель +D, контакты нумеруются справа налево: все нечетные номера сверху, а четные — снизу.

```text
33 31 ........ 5 3 1
34 32 ........ 6 4 2
```

Весь верхний ряд с нечетными номерами — это ЗЕМЛЯ (0V).

В нижнем ряду все четные номера распределены следующим образом. Примечание: NU = не используется (not used). «+» означает, что +D выводит данные или сигнал управления на дисковод, а «-» означает входной сигнал состояния привода или данные в +D.

```text
 2   NU
 4   NU
 6   NU
 8 - INDEX
10 + DRIVE ONE SELECT
12 + DRIVE TWO SELECT
14   NU
16 + MOTOR ON
18 + STEP DIRECTION
20 + STEP SIGNAL
22 + DATA OUT, WRITE
24 + WRITE GATE
26 - TRACK ZERO
28   NU
30 - DATA IN, READ
32 + SELECT SIDE
34   NU
```

Разъем на задней панели самого дисковода имеет тот же формат, за исключением того, что контакты с пометкой NU несут сигналы, которые +D не использует (например, контакт 14 может быть выбором третьего привода — drive 3 select). Естественно, направление сигналов: «+» — на дисковод, «-» — с дисковода.

Контакты находятся на уровне 5V в состоянии «выключено» / «не выбрано» и притягиваются к 0V для активации функции или выбора.

26-контактный разъем принтера также пронумерован, как описано выше, и имеет следующие соединения:  
1 — STROBE. Все нечетные с 3 по 17 включительно — биты данных от 0 до 7 соответственно. 21 — BUSY. Все четные с 2 по 22 включительно — земля (0V). Нечетные с 19 по 25 включительно, а также 24 и 26 не используются.

Конкретное имя, например `"TEST"`, выведет только программу `"TEST"`, если она есть. `"TEST*"` выведет все файлы, начинающиеся на TEST, такие как TEST1, TEST2, TESTING и так далее.

Символ `?` также может использоваться, например, `"??R*"` выведет только те файлы, у которых третья буква — «R». Напомню правила для `*` и `?`: `?` означает «здесь может быть любой один символ», а `*` означает «здесь может быть любой символ, а все последующие игнорируются». Вот почему `ERASE "*"` очищает весь диск, а символы `*` и `?` могут вызвать проблемы, если использовать их в именах файлов.

Например, пусть на диск записан файл с именем `"*this"`. Теперь попробуйте удалить его командой `ERASE "*this"`: катастрофа — пустой диск! Помните правило: `*` означает «здесь может быть все что угодно, а все остальное отбросить», то есть удаляются все файлы с любым первым символом и игнорируются все последующие.

`"?this"` удалит только `"*this"` и любое другое 5-буквенное имя, оканчивающееся на «THIS». Кстати, попробуйте на чистом диске сделать `SAVE d1 "*ONE"`. А теперь попробуйте сохранить `"*TWO"`. Система спросит, хотите ли вы перезаписать `"*ONE"`! Наверняка этому можно найти применение, но это наглядно показывает, почему `*` и `?` не следует использовать в именах файлов.
